Subject: Postdoctoral Position Available in Occupancy Change Modeling and Forecasting

Sorry for the impersonal email and feel free to circulate.

 I'm looking for a postdoctoral researcher to work with me on an exciting piece of the Grinnell Resurvey Project.  The ideal person would start before the end of the year or early next year.  Fuller description is below and attached.

Postdoctoral Position in Occupancy Change Modeling and Forecasting

A postdoctoral researcher position is available with the Grinnell Resurvey Project under the direction of Professor Steve Beissinger at UC Berkeley in the Museum of Vertebrate Zoology (MVZ) and collaborators. This project is funded by NSF to model the effects of climate and land-use change on avian communities in California at sites originally visited by Joseph Grinnell and colleagues in the early 20th century.

This position will require implementation of hierarchical multispecies occupancy models that account for imperfect detection as well as methods for forecasting the impacts of future climate and land-use change. Candidates should have experience analyzing large ecological data sets including occupancy modeling, implemented in Bayesian frameworks using Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation. Experience with land-use and climate change modeling, and machine-learning methods are a plus.

The ideal candidate will have:

-

·        A doctoral degree in a relevant subject with a strong record of scientific publications
Experience in Bayesian and high performance computing (e.g. JAGS, NIMBLE, STAN, cloud computing)
Advanced knowledge of R and additional programming languages
Skills in spatial modeling and GIS
Demonstrated ability to learn and implement new quantitative approaches and think creatively about connections between organisms, places, and people
Ability to work both independently and as part of a team

This position has flexibility for working remotely or at Berkeley, and includes competitive salary and health benefits. It is a full-time, 12-month, fixed-term position, with possible reappointment for a second year conditional on satisfactory performance and funding. Position available immediately, but will consider applicants that can not start until 2021. US citizenship or current visa required.

Review of applications begins Oct. 12  and is rolling until the position is filled. Interested candidates should send (1) an email describing their research interests and qualifications along with (2) a CV, (3) representative publications, and (4) contact information for two references to Steve Beissinger:  be...@berkeley.edu.

 Steve

messages.subject: Do I have a good model if I have to run millions of iterations?
messages.subject_clean: Do I have a good model if I have to run millions of iterations?
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am pretty new with the use of JAGS and hierarchical models. I have collected some data trough camera traps and want to perform an occupancy model. I am trying to run some models in which I use 5 covariates for the occupancy submodel and 2 for the detection submodel, nevertheless, I have had to run more than 20 millions interations to get reasonables Rhat and n.eff values. Could anyone tell me if I am doing it right?

My data consists on 63 sites (camera traps) with 14 survey ocassions (each survey ocassion = 5 days of the camera trap working fine). Although I have many NAs because the number of cameras was limited and I had to use and relocate cameras in new sites after a period of 30 days.

I would appreciate any comment or advise.

Thank you in advance.

messages.subject_clean: Do I have a good model if I have to run millions of iterations?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sandro,

Five covariates on occupancy might be a few too many for a study with 63 sites. Have you tried fitting a simpler model with a smaller number of covariates? That might be a good place to start.
If the model is still not behaving, other things to try would include centering your covariates, and trying a simpler detection model.

Cheers,

Michael

Dear all,

our new AHM2 book has officially been published yesterday. Hence, the e-book should be available immediately and the hard-copy as soon it’s delivered (haven’t seen mine yet).

Andy, Mike Meredith and I are currently updating our different webpages for the AHM book projects, as well as the R package that comes with it (AHMbook). As part of these endeavours, we have created a simple, but, we hope, informative, webpage “Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology”: www.hierarchicalmodels.com <http://www.hierarchicalmodels.com> (which then redirects to https://www.mbr-pwrc.usgs.gov/pubanalysis/roylebook/). Thanks to Jim Hines for creating and maintaining the page !

This serves as a landing page for a cluster of books on this topic and makes available additional useful resources.

Best regards  --- Marc, Andy and Mike Meredith

messages.subject: question on data setup for multi-season site occupancy models
messages.subject_clean: question on data setup for multi-season site occupancy models
messages.body_plain:
I have count data on a crustacean species.  The data were collected sporadically over a 5 year period.  That is, data were collected over multiple occasions (daily site visits) within some of the 20 seasons (5 years x 4 seasons per year) but not at all within other seasons.   Two questions on setting up a site x replicate visit x season 3-dimensional data array (patterned off of Kery and Schaub Section 13.5.2):

1.  The maximum number of daily site visits within any season was 5.  For seasons with 1-4 visits, I am assuming that NAs are entered into the count columns of the data array when they were not sampled. (?)

2. For seasons with no samples, which are chronologically after seasons that were sampled, I am assuming these these seasons are ignored rather than populating these rows in an array with NAs.

As an example of what I am proposing,  here is some fake data (below).

Regarding Question 1, season 1 had 5 repeat visits, season 2 had 2 repeat visits and season 4 had 1 visit.  The rest of the data cells in seasons 2 and 4 are populated with NAs.

Regarding Question 2, Season 3 was not sampled, so there are no rows of data.  I am uneasy about populating a season in the array with all NAs if it was sampled at all but it appears that this might be necessary to get an estimation of site-specific colonization probability over the study.

Thank you for any thoughts,
Paul Rudershausen

Thanks,

Josh

messages.subject_clean: Spatial Dependence Model, Hines et al. 2010
messages.body_plain:
Ouhhhh .... Josh,

sorry to chime in here, but I'd say that you shouldn't expect people to do all the work for you.

And especially, in my opinion, if someone finds it too hard to add covariates to a hierarchical model fit in software like JAGS, the s/he first has to get down to the basics to understand that really part of the modeling. Because if you don't, then (if you get the model to run at all), there is just far too much of a risk of fitting the wrong model (i.e., not the one you really want) or misunderstanding the meaning of the parameters.

Apologies for speaking out openly.

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.subject: Never blindly trust Rhat for convergence in a Bayesian analysis !
messages.subject_clean: Never blindly trust Rhat for convergence in a Bayesian analysis !
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

introducing a new "Cautionary Picture" feature: here is a particularly striking example of how Rhat can sometimes tell you an MCMC algorithm has converged ..... but it hasn't ! OK, this may be a pathological example, but nevertheless it's *really* good practice to always give a quick visual check to the chains for at least some key parameters in a model fit with MCMC.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: Re: Never blindly trust Rhat for convergence in a Bayesian analysis !
messages.subject_clean: Never blindly trust Rhat for convergence in a Bayesian analysis !
messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

Split-chain R-hat should detect this issue. It was introduced somewhere in Gelman's Bayesian Data Analysis book. Basically you take each MCMC chain and split it in half by iteration #, and treat each half as a separate chain. In your example you'd then probably have a large contrast between the 3 chains that came from the beginning of the original chains, and 3 chains from the end, which would result in a very large between-chain variance and a large Rhat.

This is the approach now used by rstan, but you can actually apply the relevant rstan function (rstan::monitor) to any MCMC output after a bit of formatting. For example, with jagsUI output:

library(jagsUI)
library(rstan)

data(longley)
head(longley)
gnp <- longley$GNP
employed <- longley$Employed
n <- length(employed)

data <- list(gnp=gnp,employed=employed,n=n)
modfile <- tempfile()

#Write model to file
writeLines("
model{

  #Likelihood
  for (i in 1:n){

    employed[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau)
    mu[i] <- alpha + beta*gnp[i]

  }

  #Priors
  alpha ~ dnorm(0, 0.00001)
  beta ~ dnorm(0, 0.00001)
  sigma ~ dunif(0,1000)
  tau <- pow(sigma,-2)

}
", con=modfile)

params <- c('alpha','beta','sigma')

out <- jags(data = data,
            inits = NULL,
            parameters.to.save = params,
            model.file = modfile,
            n.chains = 3,
            n.adapt = 100,
            n.iter = 1000,
            n.burnin = 500,
            n.thin = 2)

#Convert rjags mcmc.list to array format (iterations x parameters x chains)
arr <- as.array(out$samples)

#convert array to iterations x chains x parameters
arr <- aperm(arr, c(1,3,2))

#Calculate split-chain Rhat and other parameters
#no warmup/burn-in iterations saved by jagsUI, so set warmup to 0
mon <- rstan::monitor(arr, warmup=0)

I'd like to implement this in jagsUI at some point.

Ken
